text:
sara: Quick sync — I'm prototyping a "compact reservation proxy" to reduce slot fragmentation in Dedicated GPU pools. Idea: proxy hands out small "slab" credits (fractional units) backed by real GPU leases, and exposes a tiny admit API to runtime. Want feedback on operator boundary, failure modes, and rollout.

devin: Nice. Can you sketch how this differs from the existing reservoir/token-bucket admission? Is this a separate admission layer or a shim on top?

sara: It's a shim that sits between tenant-facing admission and the operator. Key differences: slabs are finer-grained (e.g., 1/8th GPU), ephemeral leases aggregated into physical leases by the proxy, and an explicit compatibility matrix for model runtime (quantized vs full). The operator only sees aggregated physical leases — proxy manages splitting/packing.

mike: Two immediate concerns: 1) KV cache + per-request memory isolation when multiple slabs map to one physical GPU; 2) eviction mechanics if proxy overcommits. How do we surface backpressure?

sara: Good catches. Plan: proxy pins KV cache per physical lease and maintains per-slab logical namespaces. If physical memory is contested we throttle admit responses and expose a `throttle-until` in the admit reply. Eviction: proxy tries soft-shrink first (merge slabs), then signal operator to scale up or migrate.

anya: For operator boundary: what surface does operator implement? Ideally: a reconciler that manages physical leases (create/destroy) and exposes metrics (utilization, slab-overhead, fragmentation). The proxy sends an intent blob to operator, not granular slab ops.

devin: That keeps operator simple, good. Metrics we need: slab-to-physical ratio, admission rejection reason counts, queued-request depth, and tail latency per-tenant. Also billing: mapping slab usage to tenant billing units.

mike: Can we keep admit API super simple, e.g.:

```
POST /admit
{
  "tenant": "acme",
  "slabs": 2,
  "qos": "p99-latency"
}
=>
{ "admitted": true, "lease_id": "L-abc123", "slab_units": 2, "throttle_until": null }
```

If throttle_until non-null runtime should fall back to slower path.

sara: Exactly. Also an endpoint to return slabs early and to heartbeat usage for accounting.

devin: Rollout strategy? Start with a canary tenant or region. We need a fallback route so requests can go either to proxy or the existing admission path.

sara: Canary first, then opt-in by tenant. Proxy will register as a routing policy: prefer-proxy, fallback-shared. We'll start with low slab density (no overcommit) then gradually increase.

anya: Observability plan: traces across proxy->operator->runtime, slab churn histogram, physical-merge events, and a simple SLO for successful admits within 50ms. Add alert for physical overcommit ratio > 0.2.

mike: Failure modes: proxy crash should not drop live leases. Need durable intent and leases in etcd/KV. Also operator must survive split/merge race — use compare-and-swap on lease-version.

sara: Agreed. Persistence + idempotent ops. Also a quick CLI for ops to force-drain a proxy node and migrate slabs to other physical leases.

deploy-bot: canary deployment started for "compact-res-proxy" in us-west-2 — build #4821

devin: One last thought: cost accounting. We must ensure slab granularity maps cleanly to billing to avoid surprises. Suggest slab-minute aggregation with rounding rules.

sara: Will add billing API contract: `/billing/usage?tenant=acme&since=...` produced by proxy aggregator. Next steps: write short RFC with API shapes, operator intent schema, and canary checklist. I'll schedule a 30m follow-up tomorrow.

mike: 👍 thanks — will draft eviction semantics doc.

anya: I'll add observability templates and alerts.

sara: Thanks all. End of thread.
